# Blagojevich denies wrongdoing, says ‘I will fight’ amid federal corruption allegations

**CHICAGO, Illinois —** Illinois Gov. Rod Blagojevich forcefully denied wrongdoing Friday and vowed to remain in office as he faced mounting pressure to resign following his arrest on federal corruption charges.

“I will fight,” Blagojevich said in his first extended public comments since federal prosecutors accused him of trying to profit from his power to appoint a successor to President-elect Barack Obama’s vacant U.S. Senate seat.

The Democratic governor, speaking at a news conference in Chicago, said he was “not guilty of any criminal wrongdoing” and urged the public not to rush to judgment based on excerpts from secretly recorded conversations cited by federal investigators.

“I’m dying to answer these charges,” Blagojevich said, but added that his attorneys had advised him not to discuss specifics of the case. “I intend to answer every allegation that comes my way.”

## Federal complaint alleges ‘pay-to-play’ scheme

Blagojevich was arrested earlier this month after federal prosecutors unveiled a criminal complaint alleging a wide-ranging corruption scheme. The most explosive allegation centered on the governor’s authority to fill Obama’s Senate seat after Obama’s election as president.

According to the complaint, Blagojevich discussed using the appointment to obtain personal benefits, campaign contributions or a high-paying job. Prosecutors quoted the governor in profanity-laced wiretap excerpts describing the Senate seat as a valuable asset.

U.S. Attorney Patrick Fitzgerald described the alleged conduct as a “political corruption crime spree,” saying investigators acted quickly in part to prevent any improper sale or trade of the Senate appointment.

Blagojevich has not been convicted of a crime. A criminal complaint contains allegations, and the governor is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

## Pressure grows from Democrats and Republicans

Since the arrest, Blagojevich has faced intense bipartisan pressure to step down. Illinois lawmakers have begun discussions on impeachment proceedings, and leading Democrats — including Obama — have called on the governor to resign.

State officials have also explored ways to limit or remove Blagojevich’s power to appoint the next senator, arguing that any selection he makes would be clouded by the allegations.

Blagojevich, however, gave no indication Friday that he planned to leave office.

“I will fight until I take my last breath,” he said, casting himself as determined to clear his name.

## Legal defense expected to challenge recordings

The governor’s legal team is expected to scrutinize the wiretap evidence and challenge the government’s interpretation of the recorded conversations. Defense attorneys often argue that excerpts from secretly recorded calls can be misleading without full context.

Blagojevich suggested Friday that the public had heard only one side of the story.

“When you hear the whole story, I’m confident that I will be vindicated,” he said.

## Political future uncertain

The allegations have plunged Illinois politics into turmoil and revived concerns about corruption in a state with a long history of public officials facing criminal investigations.

Blagojevich, who was serving his second term as governor, had already been under federal scrutiny before the Senate-seat controversy erupted. The latest complaint dramatically escalated the crisis, putting his political survival in doubt and placing state lawmakers under pressure to act.

For now, Blagojevich said he intends to remain governor while fighting the charges in court and in the arena of public opinion.

“I’m going to keep working for the people of Illinois,” he said. “I’m not going to quit.”
